title: The Packaged Breads and Cereals in Your Pantry May Be Quietly Raising Your Risk of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
excerpt: A landmark study of 124,590 adults across 21 countries found that eating five or more servings of ultra-processed foods a day nearly quadrupled the risk of developing IBD — but fresh bread and rice were protective.
body:
It is one of the quietest dietary shifts the Indian diaspora makes after settling abroad: the steel dabba of fresh roti gradually shares shelf space with sliced bread, the morning idli gives way to boxed cereal, and the pantry fills with crackers, granola bars, and packaged snack foods that barely existed in the household a generation earlier.

A sweeping new study suggests that swap may carry a serious cost — one measured not in calories or cholesterol, but in the health of the gut itself.

## What the Largest Study of Its Kind Found

Published in the *American Journal of Gastroenterology*, the research drew on data from the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study — one of the world's most ambitious population-health projects. Scientists tracked 124,590 adults living in 21 countries, spanning high-, middle-, and low-income nations, and followed them over several years to see who developed inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a group of chronic conditions that includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

The findings were stark. Participants who consumed 19 grams or more of ultra-processed grain products per day — the equivalent of a couple of slices of mass-produced bread and a handful of commercial crackers — had an 86 per cent higher risk of developing IBD than those who ate less than 9 grams per day.

When researchers widened the lens to all ultra-processed foods, the numbers climbed further. Adults eating five or more servings a day of any ultra-processed food had nearly four times the risk of IBD compared with those consuming less than one serving daily.

"By identifying specific dietary factors such as ultraprocessed grains that contribute to disease development, this provides a foundation for targeted dietary recommendations," the study's authors wrote, led by Dr. Neeraj Narula of McMaster University in Canada.

## Not All Grains Are Equal



> **"Fresh bread and rice, the staple grains of billions of people worldwide, were actually associated with a *lower* risk of IBD."**


Perhaps the study's most striking — and reassuring — detail was what it found about minimally processed grains. Fresh bread and rice, the staple grains of billions of people worldwide, were actually associated with a *lower* risk of IBD.

The implication is profound: grains are not the enemy. The industrial processing is.

Ultra-processed grain products differ from their traditional counterparts in ways that go far beyond convenience. Commercial breads often contain emulsifiers, stabilisers, added sugars, and preservatives. Packaged breakfast cereals can carry dozens of ingredients, many of them unrecognisable to anyone without a food-science degree. These additives are designed to extend shelf life, improve texture, and enhance flavour — but mounting evidence suggests they may be doing so at the expense of the gut's microbial ecosystem.

## How Processing Disrupts the Gut

Scientists believe ultra-processed foods harm digestive health through several interconnected pathways. The trillions of bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms that make up the gut microbiome — sometimes called the body's "second brain" — are exquisitely sensitive to what passes through the digestive tract.

Certain food additives, including emulsifiers like carboxymethylcellulose and polysorbate-80 that are common in processed breads and snacks, have been shown in laboratory studies to thin the protective mucus layer lining the intestines. This can allow bacteria to come into closer contact with the gut wall, triggering an immune response that, when chronic, leads to the inflammation characteristic of IBD.

Ultra-processed foods may also promote low-grade systemic inflammation throughout the body — a condition already linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain cancers — all conditions to which South Asians are disproportionately vulnerable.

## A Diaspora Blind Spot

For India's 32-million-strong global diaspora, this research hits a particularly sensitive nerve. The shift from fresh, home-cooked meals to convenience foods is one of migration's most universal dietary transitions, and it often happens gradually enough that families barely register it.

A 2019 study in *Nutrients* found that South Asian immigrants in the US and UK increased their consumption of processed and packaged foods within two to five years of arrival, while simultaneously reducing their intake of traditional legumes, fresh vegetables, and home-ground spices — the very ingredients that promote a diverse, resilient gut microbiome.

IBD rates, meanwhile, have been rising sharply in South Asian immigrant communities. Research published in *Gut* found that second-generation South Asians in the UK had IBD rates approaching or exceeding those of the white British population — a dramatic increase from the rates seen in their parents' generation and in South Asia itself.

## What the Research Suggests You Can Do

The study does not prove that ultra-processed grains directly *cause* IBD — as the researchers note, observational studies can identify associations but not definitive cause and effect. Other lifestyle factors may play a role.

But the direction of the evidence is increasingly clear, and the practical takeaways are straightforward:

- **Read the ingredient list, not just the nutrition label.** If a bread or cereal contains more than five or six ingredients, or includes emulsifiers, stabilisers, or flavour enhancers, it is ultra-processed.
- **Return to traditional staples where possible.** Fresh roti made from whole-wheat flour, steamed rice, hand-rolled parathas, idlis, and dosas are minimally processed and were associated with lower IBD risk in this study.
- **Treat packaged snacks as occasional, not routine.** Granola bars, flavoured crackers, and sweetened cereals are convenient, but they should not form the backbone of a daily diet.
- **Cook from scratch more often.** The single best way to avoid ultra-processed food is to prepare meals at home using whole, recognisable ingredients — a practice that Indian kitchens have perfected over centuries.

The study's 21-country scope and its enormous sample size make its findings difficult to dismiss. As IBD rates continue to climb in immigrant communities worldwide, the research offers a pointed reminder: what lines the pantry shelves may matter as much as what fills the plate.
